source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Empires of the Western Sudan: Ghana Empire' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/ghan/hd_ghan.htm
notes: Sumanguru, ruler of Kaniaga, captured Kumbi c.1203 after Ghana's post-Almoravid decline and loss of tributaries; Met: Ghana fell to expanding Soso. If Sosso is treated as a breakaway Ghana tributary, code T1a. Mali took over only c.1235-40.

source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, chronology 'Southeast Asia, 1400-1600 A.D.' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/08/sse.html
notes: Britannica: Muslims did not overthrow Majapahit; weakened by royal feuds and lost trade it withered away early 16th c. Met: Demak's Raden Patah also ruled Majapahit 1500-1518. Demak was a coastal former vassal (internal). Proposed end dates range 1478-1527.

successor: Hittite kingdom, Middle Kingdom phase (same monarchy)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Anatolia: The rise and fall of the Hittites' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Anatolia/The-rise-and-fall-of-the-Hittites
source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, chronology 'Anatolia and the Caucasus, 2000-1000 B.C.' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/03/waa.html
notes: Old Kingdom (c.1650-1500) is a modern periodisation; the same Hittite monarchy continued into the poorly documented Middle Kingdom and Empire. Q4: Mursili I assassinated, then succession murders before Telipinu. Core was Hattusa, not Konya Plain; Met ends Old Kingdom c.1450.

source2: Richard M. Eaton, The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204-1760, University of California Press 1993 (maps 2c-2d) - https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/view?docId=ft067n99v9
notes: Sher Khan, Afghan ruler of Bihar, took Gaur 1538 ending the Husain Shahi sultanate; Humayun briefly held Gaur 1538-39; Britannica dates conquest early 1539. Q4: Abyssinian palace coups 1486-93 (Eaton, Iranica 'Bengal i'), 1533 usurpation.

successor: Republic of Turkey (Ankara Grand National Assembly government)
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kemal Ataturk: The nationalist movement and the war for independence' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kemal-Ataturk/The-nationalist-movement-and-the-war-for-independence
notes: After defeat (Mudros 1918) Allies imposed military administration on Istanbul (Dec 1918, tightened Mar 1920); GNA abolished sultanate 1 Nov 1922. Coded T2 under priority rule; if occupation is not counted as conquest, T1c. Q4: 1908-13 coups, Arab revolt.

successor: Western Turk Khaganate itself (rival On Ok khagans) until Tang conquest 657-659
source2: E. de La Vaissiere, 'Sogdiana iii. History and Archeology', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sogdiana-iii-history-and-archeology
notes: Database end 630 (Tong Yabghu's death, civil war) is not an end: Western Turk khagans kept ruling from Semirechye, over Sogdiana, until Tang subjugation 657-659 (Britannica: 659). If 659 is taken as the end, code S1/T2 (Tang).

successor: Chuuk - Late Truk (same decentralised Chuukese communities; nominal Spanish sovereignty)
notes: No lagoon-wide central authority; 1886 matches Spain's nominal Carolines claim, not an end of any polity. Britannica: only occasional 19th-century traders and whalers; German purchase 1899, Japan 1914. Absence of central authority inferred, not stated in sources opened.

source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, chronology 'Japan, 1000-1400 A.D.' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/07/eaj.html
notes: Go-Daigo's 1331 revolt and ensuing factional war, joined by defecting bakufu vassals, destroyed the Hojo-led bakufu in 1333; emperor restored direct rule (Kemmu Restoration). All actors internal. Kyoto listed as capital; bakufu seat was Kamakura.

successor: British Protectorate of Northern Nigeria (British Empire)
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nigeria: The arrival of the British' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Nigeria/The-arrival-of-the-British
notes: Wukari passed under British Northern Nigeria c.1900; Aku Uka kept under indirect rule (Northern house of chiefs 1947). No source opened says whether by conquest or treaty; Afolayan, Encyclopedia of African History page could not be read (rate-limited).

successor: Egypt - New Kingdom Ramesside Period (19th Dynasty)
source2: Catharine H. Roehrig, 'Egypt in the New Kingdom (ca. 1550-1070 B.C.)', Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 2000 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/nking/hd_nking.htm
notes: Horemheb (c.1319-1292) was succeeded by his vizier Ramesses I, founding Dynasty 19 within the same New Kingdom state; no break in central authority. Q4: non-dynastic successions after Tutankhamun but no recorded civil war or revolt. Britannica dates transition c.1292.
